scripts.radio:
Habari za jioni. This is Kenyans Are Asking. The IMF just confirmed that Kenya has reclaimed its spot as East Africa’s largest economy in US dollar terms, overtaking Ethiopia. It looks impressive on international spreadsheets. But as we celebrate headline numbers, let us look at where public money actually bleeds. This week, government sent 84 human resource officers on compulsory leave to pave way for a probe into an alleged 6.2 billion shilling ghost-worker payroll fraud across public offices. Six point two billion shillings. That is money meant for medicine in sub-county clinics and funding public schools, quietly pocketed through phantom names. Meanwhile in Parliament, MPs are proposing tax formula cuts to bring fuel pump prices below 200 shillings per litre. The truth is simple: an expanding economy must translate into lower costs of living, affordable food, and decent public services—not bloated, corrupt payrolls. National pride is not found in dollar estimates while ordinary citizens shoulder runaway taxes to cover up internal theft.

Na kwa ufupi: Shirika la IMF linasema uchumi wa Kenya sasa ndio mkubwa zaidi Afrika Mashariki, lakini hapa nchini, maafisa themanini na nne wa HR wametumwa likizoni kupisha uchunguzi wa shilingi bilioni sita nukta mbili zilizopotea kupitia wafanyikazi hewa. Huwezi kujivunia uchumi mkubwa huku mifuko ya umma ikitoboka hivi. Ni lazima wezi wa mali ya umma wawajibishwe. Naitwa Kenyans Are Asking.
scripts.voice_note: Wadau, quick update from Kenyans Are Asking. The IMF says our economy is officially bigger than Ethiopia’s again in US dollar terms. Good headline, right? But hold on. The very same week, 84 HR officers across public offices were sent on forced leave over an alleged 6.2 billion shilling payroll fraud. Billions paid out to ghost workers while ordinary Kenyans are struggling to put food on the table, waiting for MPs to slash fuel taxes so pump prices can drop below 200 shillings. Macroeconomic rankings do not feed families. If Kenya is truly the region's powerhouse, why are billions leaking through fake payrolls while local dispensaries lack basic supplies? Let's demand real systems that track every taxpayer cent before celebrating paper growth. Share this with a friend.
scripts.sms: Usiibiwe: Sh6.2bn lost to ghost workers means starved clinics. Demand open payroll audits in public offices. Our taxes must serve real citizens, not phantoms.
scripts.reels: Eighty-four HR officers sent home. Six point two billion shillings siphoned through ghost workers. While the IMF ranks Kenya as East Africa’s largest economy, our public coffers are bleeding from inside the offices meant to safeguard them. That money could fund critical healthcare and equip classrooms. Paper growth means nothing if internal theft remains routine. Who created the ghost names, and who signed the cheques? Kenyans are asking.
